title: AI Power User: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: A workflow finishes, reports success, and produces a wrong figure with nothing flagged. Which failure does that describe?
options: A silent error, where the run fails without surfacing any warning
A hallucination, where generated text cites a source that does not exist
A mid-flow break, where the run stops before its final step
A rollback, where the workflow returns to an earlier version
questions.explanation: A silent error is defined by the absence of a signal: the process completes and reports success while the result is wrong. Loud failures announce themselves, so this kind has to be caught by checking the output rather than the status.

questions.question: A task done ten minutes every day and a task done two hours once a month both appear on an audit. Which consumes more time, and why?
options: The monthly task, because a single long session costs more than a short one
The monthly task, because infrequent work tends to be more demanding
The daily task, because frequency times duration beats a rare long block
They consume the same, because both average out over a month
questions.explanation: Total effort is frequency times duration. A small daily task adds up to more than a large monthly one, which is why an audit ranks by measured total rather than by how big a task feels.

questions.question: What is the value of keeping a changelog for a prompt or tool you reuse?
options: It records each change and its reason, so failures trace to one edit
It proves to collaborators that the work was careful, dated, and reviewed
It shows that the prompt was tested thoroughly before anyone used it
It captures every keystroke and setting so no detail is ever lost
questions.explanation: A changelog turns a degraded output into a lookup: a dated entry names the edit and the reason behind it, so the cause can be found rather than guessed. Testing and review are separate habits that a log does not replace.

questions.question: A custom tool holds three things. Which one supplies the examples, notes, and templates the tool consults so you stop re-explaining your department?
options: The tailored instructions, which set the standing format and tone
Your own project, which keeps all the chats in one place
The saved context, which holds reference material for the task
The review step, which checks each draft before it ships
questions.explanation: Saved context is the reference material, past examples, background notes, and templates, that the tool draws on across chats. Without it you would re-explain your world on every run.

questions.question: Which task belongs in the first set you automate?
options: One with the same inputs, steps, and output format on every run
One you run a few times a year but that carries high stakes
One that requires fresh judgment about what to include each time
One that depends on other people sending you material first
questions.explanation: A strong first candidate is frequent, same-shaped, and low-risk to get wrong. Work that shifts shape or needs fresh judgment has no stable frame for a saved flow to run.

questions.question: A task recurs often, but its shape changes from run to run. What is the right call?
options: Build the template anyway and force the task to fit the frame
Skip it, because a frame that keeps changing will not hold
Add more slots so every variation has its own placeholder
Build a separate template for each variation the task might take
questions.explanation: A reusable prompt pays off only when a task recurs and its frame stays stable across runs. When the shape keeps shifting, the fixed part is never reused, so the setup is wasted.

questions.question: A content workflow writes one approved long piece and then repurposes it into several shorter outputs. Where should the human review gate sit, and why?
options: After repurposing, so the gate reviews all the shorter outputs in one pass
Before repurposing, so an unchecked claim cannot spread into every output
Before drafting, so the source material is verified before any words are written
After publishing, so the gate reflects how the audience actually responded
questions.explanation: Repurposing a single source into several channels multiplies whatever it carries, so a wrong claim spreads instead of being caught once. Checking the source piece before the rewrite keeps one error from becoming several.

questions.question: A job will run once and never again. What does the assembly guidance say?
options: Build it as a pipeline anyway so the work is documented formally
Add extra steps now so individual parts can be reused later
Automate the trigger but leave the remaining steps manual
Keep it simple, since the handoffs add cost with no payback
questions.explanation: Assembly earns its cost when a job recurs with a stable shape and each step removes manual work. For a one-off, every added handoff is another thing that can break with nothing to repay it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a handover test?
options: Give the runbook entry to someone who has never run the workflow and watch where they stop, since each stop is a missing field
Confirm the workflow's runtime fits within an allowed time budget
Prove the workflow's output is identical to the manual version
Check that the trigger still fires on the correct business day
questions.explanation: A document nobody has tried to follow is a document with unknown errors in it. Watching a fresh reader stop reveals the exact fields the entry is missing, turning guesses about clarity into concrete fixes.

questions.question: Where do multi-step pipelines most often fail?
options: Inside the most complex step, where the prompt does the hardest work
At the handoff, where one step's output does not fit the next
At the trigger, because scheduled runs start at the wrong moment
At the final output, because the posting tool rejects formatted content
questions.explanation: Each step is built to consume a particular shape of input, so a change in what the previous step produces breaks the next one at the join. Naming every handoff is what turns a mysterious failure into a located one.

questions.question: What is the warning sign that a prompt's rules have become coupled?
options: The prompt runs longer than a single screen of text
The variable input sits in its own clearly labeled slot, apart from the rules
One rule appears in several sentences, so one edit touches them all
The prompt uses a delimiter that the model does not recognize
questions.explanation: Coupling means one logical rule lives in multiple places, so a single intended change forces several edits and a missed one leaves the prompt contradicting itself. Stating each rule once, in one home, is what makes an edit safe.

questions.question: A run reports success but its output is quietly wrong. Which post-run check catches this class of failure?
options: Reconciling a count in the output against the count in the source and failing the run when they disagree
Raising the retry cap so a failing step gets more attempts
Writing a more detailed prompt so the draft step makes fewer mistakes
Running the first cycles in parallel with the manual process
questions.explanation: A silent failure surfaces no error, so only a check that inspects the output afterward can catch it. Count reconciliation, field presence, and expected-content checks turn a quiet failure into a loud one.

questions.question: Two reports count the same metric differently. Why is that worse than a single wrong number?
options: Because each report becomes slower to produce when definitions differ
Because differing counts mean the underlying data must be missing
Because only one of the two reports can be published at a time
Because the disagreement leaves no basis for trusting either figure
questions.explanation: A single wrong number can be corrected against a known source, but two conflicting figures with no agreed origin leave the reader unable to choose. One agreed source and one written definition matter more than either report alone.

questions.question: Which characteristic of a step best justifies a mandatory approval before it continues?
options: The step is routine, reversible, and has behaved the same way for months
The action is hard to undo and the output goes outside the team
The step is fast and cheap, so pausing it costs almost nothing
The step produces a draft that no one reads until the following week
questions.explanation: A gate earns its interruption where a miss is costly: hard-to-undo actions, low confidence, outside visibility, or context the tool lacks. Routine and reversible steps earn rhythm instead, because gating them rebuilds the bottleneck automation removed.

questions.question: What does naming the input of a workflow give you before you run it?
options: A clear list of what to gather before the run can start
A guarantee that the tool will not need a review this time
A shorter prompt, since the tool already knows your context
A record of past runs that the tool can reuse later
questions.explanation: Input is the contract between the workflow and the rest of your work. Naming it tells you what must be in hand before a run, and a missing piece stops the run before it starts.

questions.question: A workflow completes every run without errors and its output is always neatly formatted. Why can it still be failing?
options: Because formatting is the only thing that error logs actually verify
Because a tool that completes a run has by definition produced correct output
Because output is probabilistic, so a clean run can still be wrong
Because failures only appear when a connected tool stops responding
questions.explanation: There is a gap between a workflow running and a workflow working. A model's output comes from a probability distribution, so a run can execute cleanly and be formatted correctly while the answer is quietly wrong.

questions.question: What does it mean, in plain terms, for a tool to be reliable?
options: It has never suffered a service outage
It comes from the largest and best-known vendor
Its failures can be predicted, tolerated, and recovered from
It advertises the highest uptime percentage on its landing page
questions.explanation: No tool never fails, so reliability is not about avoiding failure. A reliable tool is one whose failure you can predict, tolerate, and recover from, which is a property you can measure and plan around.

questions.question: A change to a working prompt makes its output worse. What does going back to the baseline require?
options: That the failing version is deleted before anything else is attempted
That the most recent edit is reverted by rewriting the prompt from memory
That a saved copy of the good version still exists to return to
That a new tool is chosen to replace the one that misbehaved
questions.explanation: Rollback is possible only if the known-good version was kept intact rather than overwritten, because returning to it needs a copy that still exists. Deleting the bad version or rewriting from memory does not restore the working state.

questions.question: A time audit exists to correct which specific bias in how people plan their own work?
options: People underestimate how long a single large task takes to finish
Memory inflates urgent work and hides the quiet, repetitive kind
People assume that every task they do can be automated with a tool
People overestimate how much of their week is spent in meetings
questions.explanation: Memory records what was vivid, not what consumed the most time, so it inflates urgent or interesting work and hides the routine tasks that quietly fill the week.

questions.question: Why should a post-mortem on your own failed workflow stay blameless?
options: Because blaming yourself is against company policy in most teams
Because a conclusion like 'I was careless' names nothing you can fix
Because the workflow's failure is never the builder's responsibility
Because blameless means no one is ever held accountable for a failure
questions.explanation: Blamelessness is about reaching causes you can change. A verdict of personal carelessness explains nothing and fixes nothing, while a system-level cause such as a missing check gives you something concrete to repair.

questions.question: A team is adopting one person's automation. What is the sound sequence for turning it into a shared workflow?
options: Send the whole team the record and the tool link at the same time
Adapt for a stranger, test one second user, then set the data rules
Rewrite the automation in a new tool, then document it for the team
Publish the record first, then find out who happens to use it
questions.explanation: Sharing is a packaging problem: rewrite the record so a stranger can follow it, prove it with one real second user before inviting the rest, and name the ownership and data rules it touches.

questions.question: A vendor promises a specific uptime percentage, but missing it earns only an apology, not a refund or credit. How should you classify that promise?
options: As a service level objective, a target that carries no penalty when missed
As a service level agreement, because it sets a specific number
As a service level indicator, the raw measurement of uptime
As an error budget, the amount of downtime the vendor is allowed
questions.explanation: The test is what happens if the number is missed. A financial penalty makes it an agreement; an apology with no consequence makes it an objective, even when it is advertised with a specific figure.

questions.question: A workflow's input grows past the amount of text the model can consider at once. What is the likely result, and the right fix?
options: The model silently drops or summarizes part of the input, so trim to a summary
The provider returns a rate-limit error, so space the calls out across the day
The model flags the overflow and asks for permission to continue
The workflow stops with a clear error until the input is shortened
questions.explanation: When input exceeds the context window, the model truncates or summarizes it to proceed, and that does not always announce itself. Feeding a compact summary instead of every row keeps the run inside the window.

questions.question: You keep separate copies of your house-style instructions inside each of four workflows. What does the don't-repeat-yourself principle say to do instead?
options: Keep all four, since every workflow needs its own personal copy
Delete the instructions so the tool picks whatever tone it wants
Write a longer fifth version and add it to every workflow
Keep one authoritative copy that every workflow references
questions.explanation: Duplication rots a library because a change must be made in every copy and one will be missed. Keeping a single authoritative copy that everything references means one edit fixes the behavior everywhere.

questions.question: A workflow has run for months and saves time on good days, but you keep patching it and re-checking its output. What does an honest review compare before deciding to retire it?
options: The hours it saves on its best day against a fixed monthly budget target
How often it runs against how many teammates happen to use it
The hours it returns against the time spent monitoring and fixing it
Whether it usually works against whether it is occasionally wrong
questions.explanation: Total cost of ownership weighs the hours a workflow genuinely returns against everything spent keeping it alive, and maintenance is often the largest part. When upkeep crowds out the savings, the workflow is a retirement candidate.

questions.question: For an output a downstream tool will read, what makes a fixed label shape more useful than correct prose?
options: The tool finds each value by its label instead of guessing
The prose version is usually factually wrong about the details
The labeled version needs no review before it ships downstream
The labeled version is shorter and cheaper to generate
questions.explanation: Prose is often right but unstable, with the owner or the date landing in a different place each time. Labels make every run the same shape, so nothing downstream has to hunt or guess.

questions.question: Which element makes a decision record genuinely useful to a future reader?
options: A detailed narrative of every option you considered and rejected
A manager's signature confirming the choice was authorized
The condition under which you would reverse the decision
A screenshot of the settings so they can be reproduced
questions.explanation: The value of a record sits in its reversal condition. A decision with no stated condition for changing it can only be argued about, while one that says what would change your mind can be revisited honestly.

questions.question: A workflow is refused after several calls in a row, even though plenty of daily allowance remains. What limit was hit, and how should it be handled?
options: A context window limit, so the input should be shortened before retrying
A spend limit, so the monthly cap should be raised before continuing
A rate limit on requests per minute, so pace the calls out over time
A quality regression, so the workflow should be rolled back to a prior version
questions.explanation: Rate limits are measured across requests per minute and tokens per minute, so you can be blocked on requests while your token allowance is untouched. Because the work need not run in one burst, pacing the calls is the fix.

questions.question: Which description captures automation bias?
options: Favoring a system's suggestion over correct information elsewhere
Distrusting a system's suggestion even when that output is correct
Assuming every automated system will eventually fail on its own
Preferring to hand a task to a person even when a tool does it well
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the habit of favoring an automated system's suggestion over other information, even when the other information is correct. It appears both as failing to notice a problem and as following a wrong suggestion against the evidence.

questions.question: A gate approved cleanly for months starts getting signed off without a real read. What is the structural defense?
options: Add a second approval step from the same reviewer on every run
Remove the gate, since a reliable workflow no longer needs one
Run the workflow less often so each review feels more significant
Put the deciding evidence in front of the reviewer at the gate
questions.explanation: Complacency grows as a system proves reliable, so willpower is a weak defense. Designing the pause so the evidence needed to decide arrives in one place, and the check cannot be bypassed, makes a genuine review the easiest path.

questions.question: What makes a run of a workflow a dry run?
options: It produces full output, then stops before anything is sent or changed
It runs on invented sample data so that the real records are never touched
It sends the output to one test recipient before the full list
It skips the output checks entirely so the workflow finishes faster
questions.explanation: A dry run uses the real input and produces the real result, then halts before any send, post, schedule, or record change. Substituting fake data or partially sending misses the point: the value is seeing the genuine output at zero consequence.

questions.question: A post-mortem reaches a clear root cause but produces no assigned fixes. Why does this fall short?
options: Because the timeline alone is the real output of a post-mortem
Because action items only matter when a whole team runs the workflow
Because conclusions with no owners and deadlines are a story, not a fix
Because a root cause does not need to be written down once it is understood
questions.explanation: The follow-up actions are the point of the exercise. Without specific fixes carrying owners and deadlines, the review documents what happened but does nothing to stop it from happening again.

questions.question: Why pin a limited field, such as priority, to a fixed set of allowed values?
options: It lets the tool invent a value whenever one is missing
It removes the need to define that field inside the prompt at all
It keeps values consistent so a tool can sort and filter cleanly
It makes the output shorter for a human to read
questions.explanation: An open text field collects different spellings and formats that a tool cannot group. Allowed values keep every run inside the same set, which is what makes sorting and filtering work.

questions.question: What turns a group of separate apps into a single connected workflow?
options: Each app is opened from one shared dashboard window
One app hands its output straight to the next one
Every app is set to run on the same schedule each week
A person copies the results between the apps in order
questions.explanation: A connected workflow is a chain joined by handoffs, where each step passes its output to the next without a person relaying it. Copying by hand is the manual work the connection replaces.

questions.question: What distinguishes human-in-the-loop oversight from human-on-the-loop oversight?
options: A person watches a dashboard and steps in only when an exception appears
A person checks the output after the workflow has already finished
A person must approve the output before the workflow can continue
A person builds the workflow and then leaves it to run untouched
questions.explanation: In the loop means the human decision sits inside the path, so nothing proceeds until someone authorizes it. On the loop means the workflow executes on its own while a person watches and intervenes afterward.

questions.question: How does a shared workflow turn into shadow AI?
options: It is shared through a free tool the organization never paid for
Its output differs slightly from the manual process for the same input
It runs on company data with no owner, no version, and no data rules
It is run by more than three people on the same day
questions.explanation: Shadow AI is an AI process running outside approved governance and oversight. Once a workflow touches company data with no named owner, no version, and no rules on what it may read, sharing has become a risk the organization cannot see.

questions.question: Which report is the weakest candidate for building a workflow?
options: A weekly report that leadership reads and acts on
A monthly report drawn from a stable, agreed source
A one-time analysis for a decision already made
A daily report with a fixed set of fields
questions.explanation: A workflow pays off when a job recurs, keeps a stable shape, and produces output someone acts on. A one-time analysis fails all three, so the structure would add maintenance with nothing to return.

questions.question: Two hundred submissions land in one hour and the workflow cannot keep pace. What does a queue do?
options: It processes the whole pile at once so the backlog clears immediately
It drops the excess items so the workflow stays within capacity
It lines work up in arrival order and clears it at a steady pace
It converts the schedule into an event trigger for future runs
questions.explanation: A queue absorbs the gap between how fast work arrives and how fast it can be handled, holding items in order until they are processed. Handling the spike all at once or dropping items is the failure a queue exists to prevent.

questions.question: A workflow's output changes even though the tool, prompt, and input are all the same. What is this called?
options: A tool update, because the app shipped a new version
A deprecation, because the vendor is retiring a feature
Behavior drift, because the model behind it changed
A data error, because the input files no longer match
questions.explanation: Behavior drift is the same tool, prompt, and input producing different output because the model underneath was swapped. It is silent, and only a saved baseline lets you tell it apart from your own mistake.

questions.question: While writing a runbook entry you are not sure what triggers an automation, only that it runs most mornings. What should you do?
options: Write down a plausible trigger so the entry looks finished and complete
Leave the trigger section out so the entry stays short and easy to update
Write that the trigger is unknown and then go check it
Remove the automation from your stack since you cannot describe it
questions.explanation: A truthful entry with a gap is a roadmap, while a polished entry with a silent guess is a trap. Recording the unknown and verifying it keeps the record honest and useful.

questions.question: A tool writes a fluent paragraph with a citation to a source. What check actually catches fabrication?
options: Asking the tool whether the citation is accurate
Checking the specific claim against the original source
Re-running the same prompt and comparing the two outputs
Judging whether the paragraph reads confidently and smoothly
questions.explanation: Confidence is the tell, not the evidence: fluent text can surround an invented citation. Only verifying the specific claim against a source you can inspect separates real support from fabricated support.

questions.question: Why does a connected chain need a human review at its end?
options: Because integrations can run only after a person approves the trigger
Because downstream apps reject output that a person has not read
Because an error early in the chain flows into every later step
Because no-code tools cannot run the same chain twice
questions.explanation: A mistake in one link makes every later link wrong, and the final result still looks confident. The review is the point where a person catches that before it ships.

questions.question: What does a custom tool change about the review step?
options: Nothing: it drafts faster and better shaped but still errs sometimes
It removes the review, because the saved instructions prevent errors
It moves the review inside the tool, which checks its own output
It makes the review optional for low-stakes runs only
questions.explanation: A custom tool saves the re-deciding, not the checking. The output still needs a person to confirm it before it ships, because a confident draft can still be wrong.

questions.question: What does dividing a prompt into labeled sections actually accomplish?
options: It lets the model and a reader tell rules from context and data
It makes the prompt shorter and cheaper to send on every single run
It removes any need to test the prompt after it is changed
It lets the same prompt run on any model without further edits
questions.explanation: Structure marks which text is instruction, which is context, and which is variable input, so the model reads each part correctly and a reader can see where to edit. The gain is legibility and safe editing, not brevity or portability.

questions.question: Once the standing instructions and reference material are saved, what does each new run of the workflow need from you?
options: The full prompt restated each time, so the tool stays aligned
A fresh copy of the background material pasted in for the tool
A new format choice each run, since the old one no longer applies
Just the fresh facts for that run, with the rest in place
questions.explanation: The saved setup carries the format, tone, and background, so the input shrinks to the new facts. That reduction is the payoff, because the decisions are made once instead of weekly.

questions.question: Which task is the clearest candidate to keep manual rather than run unattended?
options: A low-stakes summary that review would cost more than it saves
A decision that is costly to make wrong and hard to undo
A routine update that a person can reverse as easily as it was made
A recurring job that runs on a fixed schedule with stable inputs
questions.explanation: The test is how much a wrong result costs and how hard it is to undo. When both are high, keep the task manual or let automation run only up to the decision point where a person signs off.

questions.question: What does naming each boundary buy when you assemble a pipeline?
options: It removes the need for any human review gate anywhere in the flow
It makes the pipeline run faster because steps can overlap
It exposes a broken join at a named boundary, not downstream
It guarantees that no step will produce unexpected output
questions.explanation: Writing down what a step produces and what the next step needs makes the interface explicit. When a shape changes, the failure appears at the boundary you named rather than as odd behavior blamed on the wrong step.

questions.question: Why does building a workflow get cheaper over time once you keep a library of reusable pieces?
options: Because you memorize each workflow and can rebuild it from memory
Because each new workflow starts from proven pieces instead of a blank page
Because the tools themselves get faster the more you use them
Because repeating the same task daily builds speed through habit
questions.explanation: Compounding happens when the pieces from finished work feed back into the next effort. Reusing proven templates, contracts, and connectors means the next workflow starts from working parts instead of re-solving problems you already solved.

questions.question: A report feeds a decision that is made once a week. What cadence fits it best?
options: A weekly run timed to finish before the decision is made
An hourly run so the figures are always as fresh as possible
A daily run so a full week of data is never out of date
A run every time the source data changes, regardless of use
questions.explanation: Cadence should match how often the output is actually used, not how fast it could run. A weekly decision needs a run timed before it, and more frequent runs spend effort on results nobody consumes.

questions.question: What turns a review habit into a true gate?
options: Adding a second person to look at the draft as well
Sending a reminder on the morning the output is due
Moving the review earlier so there is more time to fix problems
Naming the checks, blocking delivery when one fails, recording the decision, and setting a due time
questions.explanation: A gate is built into the workflow rather than bolted on. It names the specific checks, stops delivery when one fails, records the decision, and has an owner and a deadline, so a bad output cannot proceed.

questions.question: A minor patch ships for a tool, and a smoke test shows your workflow still returns the expected output. What is the right response?
options: Reword the prompt anyway, since every update should be treated as a reason to change
Ride it out, since a verified change that does not affect output needs no action
Retire the workflow, because any change to a tool is a sign it is no longer worth keeping
Stop running smoke tests, since a passing test means the test is no longer needed
questions.explanation: A change that a smoke test confirms does not affect your workflow needs no action. The discipline is to confirm that with the test rather than assume it, since riding out an unchecked change is neglect.

questions.question: When designing a pipeline, what is the cheapest way to catch a mismatch between two steps before you wire anything?
options: Run all the steps together and see which one breaks first
Add error handling to every step before the first run
Write out each step's input, action, and output in order and compare the seam between them
Wire in the schedule so real runs surface the problem
questions.explanation: One step's output is the next step's input, so writing them down together exposes a seam where the shapes do not line up. Catching that on paper costs minutes, while catching it in a broken run costs far more.

questions.question: What does staying accountable for an AI-drafted output actually require of you?
options: Sending it as soon as the tool reports that it is confident
Reviewing it only when the task feels unusually risky that day
Adding a disclaimer so readers know a tool wrote the draft
Checking it at the moment a wrong result still matters
questions.explanation: Accountability means a person stays in the loop at the moment the output could still be wrong, since the tool drafts but you decide what actually ships.

questions.question: Which protection gives the earliest warning against a workflow quietly running up a large bill?
options: A larger context window, so the workflow stops trimming its input
A monthly spend alert that notifies you before the cap is reached
A higher requests-per-minute limit, so bursts finish faster
A smaller golden set, so fewer check runs are made each week
questions.explanation: A spend alert notifies you as tracked spend climbs, while a hard cap stops requests once the limit is hit. A cap you set yourself is the cheapest insurance against a bill that grows without erroring.

questions.question: When a vendor's marketing promise and its observed history of incidents disagree, which should guide your decision?
options: The promise, since the vendor knows its own systems best
The track record, because observed behavior is what your future will repeat
Neither, since no vendor's claims can ever be checked
Whichever is more recent, since both can change over time
questions.explanation: Observed behavior over time is the strongest evidence you can have, while a promise is only a hypothesis about the future. When the two disagree, size your dependence on what the tool has actually done, not on what it says it will do.

questions.question: Why should a recurring content workflow pull its plan from one shared calendar rather than a personal list?
options: A personal list is slower to update than a shared calendar is
Two versions of the plan drift, so the flow acts on stale data
A shared calendar writes the first draft of each piece automatically
A personal list cannot record which channel a piece is meant for
questions.explanation: A single source of truth prevents divergence. With two versions of the plan, the workflow eventually works from outdated information and drafts cancelled pieces or skips newly added ones.

questions.question: A workflow handles normal input correctly but miscounts when a field arrives unusually long. What does that illustrate?
options: A happy-path run, because normal inputs behave as expected
An edge case, a failure at the boundary of the input range
A rollback, because an earlier version of the prompt was restored
A dry run, because output was produced without being sent anywhere
questions.explanation: An edge case is a problem that appears only at an extreme of the operating range rather than in normal use, so correct ordinary runs say nothing about it. Deliberately feeding the awkward input is what surfaces the failure.

questions.question: Why define the desired output before running a workflow?
options: So the tool can be given fewer instructions to follow each time
So the review step can be skipped once the format matches
So the run finishes faster on a repeated task
So you can tell a good result from a bad one when it arrives
questions.explanation: An output described in advance, with its format, length, and sections, gives you the standard to judge against. Without it, any draft looks acceptable because nothing defines acceptable.

questions.question: A draft comes back with a confident statistic and no indication of where the number came from. What is the sound way to handle it?
options: Add a prompt rule that forbids the draft from using any statistics
Publish it whenever the figure sounds plausible and matches industry norms
Trace the number to a source you can check, and cut it if none exists
Soften the wording so the claim reads as an estimate rather than a fact
questions.explanation: A plausible, neatly formatted number with no traceable source is fabricated rather than verified. The dependable fix is a checking habit at the review gate, not another prompt rule.

questions.question: What makes a why-line beside a rule worth writing?
options: It repeats the instruction in different words so the model notices it
It records why the rule exists so a reader can judge if it holds
It proves the rule was written by a person rather than generated
It keeps the rule from being changed without a second approval
questions.explanation: A comment preserves the reason behind a rule, which is the knowledge that disappears first and the thing needed to decide whether the rule can change. Restating the rule adds no information, and duplicating it couples the parts.
